findings.title: Any holder of 1,000,000 DEAD can take the PoolManager's whole DEAD balance on Base after 90 days without a payout, and one account did so on 17 November 2026
findings.difference: The cause is a token rule, and Base is where the token and its pools are. DeadToken at 0xf0197f10ea542a67914ecc0ec5304dc9df1faf6f lets any caller who holds 1,000,000 DEAD call claimIdleTokens(target) and move the whole balance of an address that has sent no DEAD for 90 days: half to the caller, 40 percent burned and 10 percent to three platform addresses. The token keeps a whitelist of pool addresses that are exempt, and the Uniswap v4 PoolManager is not on it. Earlier cycles recorded balances that rise through a public trigger (F-041, F-066, F-067). This is a public trigger that lowers a balance that pools have recorded.
findings.mechanism: 1. Core keeps no per currency total. A pool's reserves are numbers in pool state, and the only place the token balance is read is sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-365). When the balance falls without a take, every later take of that currency draws on less than pools record, and the transfer in take reverts once the balance is too low (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). 2. DeadToken updates lastTransferTime only for the sender of a transfer, and for a receiver whose balance was zero (verified source Dead.sol lines 563 to 578). The PoolManager is a sender only when a take pays DEAD out. A quiet period of 90 days without a DEAD payout makes the whole pooled balance claimable (lines 388 to 420: balance check of the caller at 390, whitelist check at 394, idle check at 398, 50 percent to the caller at 405 and 413, 40 percent burned at 406 and 414). 3. Observed: transaction 0xc32384b25be1e5d29cd5e978fc5f531359ddd8dcae67a1ff89204e98c27d0d2b in Base block 58,594,779 (17 November 2026, 09:55:31 UTC) is a contract creation by 0x5f21bfbe94a4774fc6fb88ac84d47538422f7976. The new contract 0x25bead0f62a7c234e89691e4519ca5e74079cf3f receives 1,000,000 DEAD from the pair 0x098a1a39a006ea83c86fd8da991c0e7134eaf68c, emits three TokensClaimed logs (targets 0x50ddc37e9060fda26cc5fe2f521fe9d01bc29810 for 18,583.25 DEAD, the PoolManager for 14,899.78 DEAD and 0xaa2e244d93fd4d0d8a6c6d525de06468d77be7b3 for 13,444.75 DEAD) and returns 1,003,009.03 DEAD to the pair. The PoolManager emitted no log in that transaction. Its DEAD balance was 14,899.783090229956530365 at block 58,594,778 and 0 at block 58,594,779. lastTransferTime(PoolManager) one block earlier was 1784165391, which is 10,743,940 seconds (124 days) before the block. 4. The PoolManager took no part in the call. No sync, settle, take or unlock is needed, so no check in core can see it. 5. The balance does not come back. Three later swaps paid 88.41, 699.16 and 872.46 DEAD into the PoolManager, which holds 1,660.03 DEAD today. Those tokens are recorded by pools as well, so the gap of 14,899.78 DEAD stays.
findings.impact: 14,899.78 DEAD left the PoolManager: 7,449.89 to the claimer, 5,959.91 burned and 1,489.98 to the three platform addresses. I found no price source for DEAD and did not value it. The liquidity of the pools on the routes of the DEAD swaps before and after the claim is unchanged across the claim block (for example pool id 0x18fca1729428c26f554c4f431a551e05404b0d6b8ae9ae518966e5a9e9371121 holds liquidity 319,322,205,084,229 at block 58,594,778 and today), so pools still record the DEAD that was taken. Liquidity providers and buyers in the DEAD pools lose: a swap or a removal that must pay out more DEAD than the PoolManager holds reverts. The loss is limited to currency DEAD, because deltas, takes and settles are kept per currency (src/PoolManager.sol:368-378). Pools in other tokens are not touched. The token saw 136 TokensClaimed logs since block 56,000,000, so claiming idle holders is routine for this token.
findings.preconditions: A DEAD balance of 1,000,000 for the length of one call, which the observed account borrowed from a pair inside its creation transaction. No DEAD payout from the PoolManager for 90 days. The PoolManager stays off the token's pool whitelist (whiteListedPool(PoolManager) returns 0 and getPoolWhitelistStatus(PoolManager) returns false, false and 0). After the claim the timer restarted when the PoolManager received DEAD into a zero balance at timestamp 1795149430 (20 November 2026), and getTimeUntilClaimable(PoolManager) returned 7,502,995 seconds at my read, so the balance becomes claimable again on about 18 February 2027 unless a take pays DEAD out before then. I did not read the PoolKey of the DEAD pools (the Base log endpoint serves 1,000 blocks per request), so the list of pools comes from the Swap logs of the transactions that moved DEAD, and I did not send any transaction.
findings.mitigations: The token admin can put the PoolManager on the pool whitelist with setWhiteListPool, which takes effect after a 60 minute timelock (Dead.sol lines 315 to 324 and 355 to 382). Any account can restart the timer by causing a DEAD payout from the PoolManager, for example a swap that buys a small amount of DEAD. Liquidity providers should not pool a token that lets third parties move idle balances. Interfaces can find such tokens with the search of this unit: an ERC-20 Transfer log with the PoolManager as sender in a transaction where the PoolManager emitted no log. Core cannot prevent it, because the token moves the balance without calling the PoolManager.

findings.title: Token contracts have burned or moved the PoolManager's balance of their own token on six networks, and hookless pools with active liquidity now record tokens the PoolManager does not hold
findings.difference: The cause is token code written by the token's author, on the networks where pool creation is cheapest and most used. These tokens can change balanceOf(PoolManager) without any call from the PoolManager: a transferFrom that skips the allowance for chosen senders, an allowance from the PoolManager that the token writes by itself, a controller contract that rewrites balances, or an owner burn. F-069 recorded tokens whose balance falls with time. These fall in one transaction, to zero in 20 of the 53 confirmed cases on Ethereum.
findings.mechanism: 1. The PoolManager can only call transfer and balanceOf on a currency (src/types/Currency.sol:60-73, 94). It never approves anyone. A fall of its balance in a transaction where it emits no log is therefore the token's own doing. 2. Search: every ERC-20 Transfer log with the PoolManager as sender and the zero address, 0x...dEaD, 0xdead000000000000000042069420694206942069 or address 1 as recipient, over the block ranges in the sources. For each token, receipts of up to six such transactions were read, and for tokens with a hit where the PoolManager emitted no log, every hit. Each flagged token was then checked by balanceOf(PoolManager) one block before and at the block of one example. 3. Results. Ethereum: %s rows over %s tokens, %s tokens flagged, %s confirmed by a balance fall and %s that only emit a log (spoof tokens). BNB Smart Chain: %s rows, %s tokens, %s flagged, %s confirmed. Polygon: 5 flagged, 4 confirmed, of which PolySata and SNI have pools and two are spam tokens without a pool. Unichain: 13 flagged, 1 confirmed (ELX), 12 spoof. Elysium: 3 flagged and confirmed (CLU, EMBR, BLOB). Arbitrum One: 5 flagged and confirmed, one of them the issuer burn of PUSD that is filed as its own finding. 4. Forms seen. (a) A helper contract reads balanceOf(PoolManager) and calls transferFrom(PoolManager, 0xdead, amount) on the token; the token logs Approval(PoolManager, helper, 0) afterwards, so it had written an allowance in the PoolManager's name. Ethereum helper 0xd8e11826e82619bf49c58c05f26c8e00b0b64ea4 with selector 0x73ed6b13 did this for %s of the confirmed tokens, and the same selector appears for %s confirmed tokens on BNB Smart Chain (15 of them through 0xa25c886dced0e8fc0129082bf597381ea073c925). (b) An externally owned account calls transferFrom(PoolManager, 0xdead, amount) on the token directly. For CLU on Elysium I read the runtime bytecode: after the balance update the transfer routine loads a flag for tx.origin and, when it is set, returns true at once, which skips the allowance spending in transferFrom. A read-only transferFrom(PoolManager, other, 1000) reverts with ERC20InsufficientAllowance from an unrelated address and succeeds from the original sender 0xd27d278469aa24b5e8ed3af8675d5f6c2548f884. (c) TRUMP MAGA on Ethereum (verified source): transfer() only calls _beforeTokenTransfer, which emits the log and forwards to an unverified controller (lines 505 to 508 and 652), and cap() lets that controller emit any Transfer log (lines 680 to 688). In transaction 0xa6ce9d53504d62a54600498895c8671eb13fb8f312cdbb9d3a4fa345f0d89003 a holder's transfer of 90,100 MAGA made the controller call token function 0x20bd4fca, and the PoolManager's balance went from 776,894.03 MAGA to 0. Nine such events since block 21,818,333 removed 25,231,970 MAGA. (d) Owner functions such as burn(address,uint256) and burnFrom(address,uint256). 5. Effect in core: take pays out with transfer and reverts when the balance is too low (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). A holder of a positive delta in that token can still close it with mint or clear (src/PoolManager.sol:310-329), so a removal of liquidity can succeed when the caller gives up or defers the token side.
findings.impact: Pools that still have active liquidity while the PoolManager holds none of the token: TRUMP MAGA on Ethereum (balance 0; pools 0x4686f189f970... with liquidity 52,818,877,641,898,785 and 0x03762bf00ac1... with 1,320,363,208,123,135,774, both paired with ETH and without a hook), MEME 0x05f226755b11cb3666340551ebbaa615cdfefdd6 and BITCOIN 0x37d299d9900209c3566254cfe59bfe6ff8f8c295 on Ethereum, ELX 0x6836567f23a137f2ed07576826b0d2579b416b6d on Unichain, and SNI 0xdc685acc53ca2a760029cab2f6a587482aa9cf57 on Polygon with a balance of 1 base unit. For the other confirmed tokens I checked the balance fall and not the pools. Buyers of such a token cannot be paid, and liquidity providers cannot take the token side. Whoever holds the token outside the PoolManager can still sell it into the pool for the other currency. The amounts are in tokens without a price source, so I did not value them. The shortfall stays inside each token's own currency id; pools of other tokens are not affected. The victims chose a pool with a token written by the party that gains.
findings.preconditions: A pool in a token whose author kept a path to the PoolManager's balance. The actor is the token author or an account the token treats as privileged. For form (c) the trigger was an ordinary holder's transfer, and the rule sits in a controller whose code is not public. On BNB Smart Chain the Initialize query failed (limit exceeded), so the number of pools per token is not known there. The Base, World Chain and Robinhood Chain searches cover recent windows only (blocks from 57,500,000, 34,000,000 and 109,000,000) and X Layer 400,000 blocks. Monad, OP Mainnet, Avalanche, Ink, Celo, Arc, Soneium, Zora, MegaETH, Tempo and HyperEVM were searched over the whole history and have no confirmed case. The search sees burns only. A forced transfer to an ordinary recipient shows up only in the census windows of this unit (0.5 to 30 days per network), where none was found.
findings.mitigations: Core cannot stop a token from changing its own ledger. Interfaces and routers can flag a token when balanceOf(PoolManager) falls in a transaction without a PoolManager log, which the scripts scan_burns.py, classify_burns.py and validate_burns.py in the work directory detect. Liquidity providers in such a pool can still recover the other currency with a router that closes the token side by mint or clear. A deployer who wants a hard guarantee needs per currency reserve accounting, which this code does not have.

findings.title: The owner of Pleasing USD burned 41,000 PUSD out of the Arbitrum One PoolManager balance with an owner only burnFrom
findings.difference: F-036 and F-028 record that an issuer can block or burn the single address that holds every pool's balance. This is a case where an issuer did it. PUSD at 0xc8fb643d18f1e53698cfda5c8fdf0cdc03c1dbec on Arbitrum One is an upgradeable token whose owner can call burnFrom(address,uint256) on any holder.
findings.mechanism: 1. On 23 April 2026 the owner 0x43f285d7d53cc3e7bd4914d3e57ec90f58f510ff sent burnFrom(PoolManager, 40,000 PUSD) in block 455,597,235 (transaction 0x077516739f49e38972552537bbc49fe61e542dd6ca0b3d4d0ada8c3cf1de8fe6) and burnFrom(PoolManager, 1,000 PUSD) in block 455,604,741 (transaction 0x86afa98aa0369719d0faeda5dce5a1708fd6acc0e054b75f4287523b4f54e8c9). The PoolManager's balance went from 44,024.91 to 4,024.91 PUSD and from 1,509.05 to 509.05 PUSD. 2. The PoolManager emitted no log in either transaction. Pool state was not changed, so pools kept recording the burned tokens. 3. A read-only burnFrom(PoolManager, 1) from an unrelated address reverts with the text Ownable: caller is not the owner. From the owner it reverts today with the text blacklist, so the burn needs the target on a list that the owner controls. 4. Thirteen pools name PUSD, ten of them created between blocks 455,516,336 and 455,554,073, in the hours before the burns, with fees of 9 to 80 percent. Eight still show liquidity. The PoolManager holds 14.14 PUSD today.
findings.impact: 41,000 PUSD of the PoolManager's balance was destroyed. The first burn took 40,000 of the 44,024.91 PUSD it held. I did not establish who the liquidity providers were or why the owner acted, and I found no price source. Whoever held a position or a claim in PUSD at that time could no longer be paid in full by take. The other currencies of those pools were not touched by the burn.
findings.preconditions: Control of the token owner account, and the PoolManager on the token's blacklist at the time of the call. The implementation behind the proxy was not read; the statements about the owner check and the blacklist rest on the revert texts of two eth_call tests and on the two transactions.
findings.mitigations: None in core. Pool creators and liquidity providers should treat an owner burn function as a risk to every pool of that token, and interfaces can show it. The search of this unit lists such burns after the fact.

For a recent window on each network: every ERC-20 Transfer log with the PoolManager as sender or recipient, every wrapper Deposit log that names it, and every PoolManager log. A row is flagged when the transaction holds no Swap, ModifyLiquidity or Donate log and the PoolManager pays out or mints more of a token than it receives or burns as claims. With ordinary tokens core cannot produce such a row (src/PoolManager.sol:112, 291-297, 322-336, 349-365).
cleared.result: Windows and flagged rows: Ethereum 3.0 days, 343,301 transactions, 1 rows; Optimism 7.0 days, 372,638 transactions, 17 rows; Base 0.5 days, 116,857 transactions, 0 rows; Unichain 7.0 days, 369,767 transactions, 0 rows; Zora 30.0 days, 289 transactions, 0 rows; Worldchain 2.0 days, 8,397 transactions, 0 rows; Ink 7.0 days, 124,496 transactions, 0 rows; Soneium 30.0 days, 50,788 transactions, 0 rows; Celo 30.0 days, 4,496 transactions, 0 rows; X Layer 2.0 days, 45,345 transactions, 0 rows; Arbitrum One 7.0 days, 230,766 transactions, 18 rows; Robinhood Chain 1.0 days, 436,797 transactions, 0 rows; Elysium 3.0 days, 133,881 transactions, 0 rows; Polygon 7.0 days, 195,562 transactions, 50 rows; BNB Smart Chain 1.0 days, 315,577 transactions, 393 rows; Avalanche 14.0 days, 64,632 transactions, 0 rows; Monad 1.0 days, 79,232 transactions, 0 rows; MegaETH 30.0 days, 12,416 transactions, 0 rows; Tempo 30.0 days, 9,968 transactions, 0 rows; Arc 3.0 days, 240,107 transactions, 126 rows; HyperEVM 30.0 days, 1,318 transactions, 0 rows. All flagged rows are explained. OP Mainnet (17 rows) and Arbitrum One (18 rows) are one transaction each in which the protocol fee controller collects fees: the OP Mainnet trace shows 18 calls of collectProtocolFees from 0xd85393784234fb2ee4f077867a8b78e1ad4ce56b, and on Arbitrum One protocolFeesAccrued for USDC and ARB one block earlier equals the amounts paid out. Polygon: 28 sLGNS and 21 sATH claim mints (F-066) and one spoof token. Ethereum: the MAGA burn that is filed as a finding. Arc: 126 rows are native payouts that Arc logs at 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe, and each is matched by an ERC-6909 burn of id 0 or of the USDC face id in the same transaction. BNB Smart Chain: 393 rows over 134 tokens, of which 132 are called with the selector 0x7111a994, transfer(address[],address[],uint256[]), to emit Transfer logs with arbitrary senders (the rows I printed carry the symbol U5DT and one sender); the two others emit such logs through transferFrom calls of a helper. For 133 of them the balance could not be read at the old block, so the spoof label rests on the call pattern. No row shows a take of a token followed by a larger credit without a matching transfer, and no row shows a payout of the surplus of a rebase by take. The method cannot judge transactions that also hold a pool event.

cleared.check: Part (b) of lead L-318: transactions in which the PoolManager pays a token out and receives it back (flash use of take), and whether the token is one whose balance moves without transfers.
cleared.result: Round trips are common and use ordinary tokens. Round trips without a pool event in the windows: Ethereum 7,815 (WETH 3,405, USDC 1,802, USDT 1,039), OP Mainnet 74,789, Avalanche 13,353, Robinhood Chain 11,443, BNB Smart Chain 7,539, Base 7,146, Polygon 5,942, Elysium 4,274, Arbitrum One 3,476, Ink 3,008, Monad 1,685, X Layer 1,186. I compared the tokens with the lists of cycle 4 of tokens whose balance does not reconcile with Transfer logs. The only tokens in both lists with a round trip outside a pool event are wrapped native tokens (WETH, WBNB and WMON, whose Deposit logs explain the mismatch), the native mirror of Arc, and stETH with four round trips on Ethereum. The traced stETH case (0xe86b4759a83704c42257981142044756ee2f78a8387696314ecff8963c54f423) is an EIP-7702 account that sends stETH through sync and settle and takes it back with 1 wei less, with no call that changes the stETH supply in between. sLGNS has three round trips in the Polygon window, all in transactions that also hold a pool event, which this method cannot judge. sATH, sKLIMA, USDI and AMPL have none.

cleared.check: Tokens that emit Transfer logs with the PoolManager as sender while its balance does not fall.
cleared.result: These are spoof tokens used for address poisoning and fake airdrops, and they hold no pool funds. Confirmed by balanceOf(PoolManager) before and at the block: 25 tokens on Ethereum, 12 on Unichain, 6 on BNB Smart Chain, 1 each on Polygon, OP Mainnet and Robinhood Chain. Example: 0x20204018a5a97149168faa73477bd5db9756a141 on Polygon, whose name is USDC with invisible characters. Any monitor that reads Transfer logs to track the PoolManager must check balances as well.

cleared.check: Whether the public rebase triggers known from cycle 4 were booked as claims anywhere else: sNVB and sSAC on BNB Smart Chain (the earlier search covered 1,344,000 blocks), USDI and AMPL on Ethereum.
cleared.result: No. BNB Smart Chain: 800,303 claim mints in blocks 45,369,483 to 135,230,263, 17,807 receipts read over 2,291 pairs, none unexplained, and no outflow in the one day census other than the spoof logs. Ethereum: 1,985,249 claim mints, 42,742 receipts over 6,087 pairs, none unexplained, and one flagged row in the three day census (MAGA). The surplus of these tokens is still unclaimed or was taken in a form that leaves no claim log outside the census windows.

leads.question: Run the census of this unit (Transfer logs that name the PoolManager joined with PoolManager logs per transaction) over the whole history of each network with an indexed log source, and list every transaction where the PoolManager's balance of a token falls without a PoolManager log, whatever the recipient.
leads.why: The full history search of this unit sees only burns. The DEAD case on Base was found because 40 percent of the claim is burned. A token that lets a third party move the PoolManager's balance to an ordinary address is visible only in the windows of 0.5 to 30 days.

leads.question: List pooled tokens that have a public function which moves or burns another holder's balance (idle claims, inactivity decay, reflection sweeps, liquidation of dormant accounts), and test with a read-only call from an unrelated address whether the PoolManager is a valid target today.
leads.why: claimIdleTokens of DeadToken on Base is such a function and an ordinary account used it against the PoolManager. Tokens of the same template may exist on other networks, and the PoolManager is idle for any token whose pools see no payout.

leads.question: Finish the burn search for the whole history of Base, Robinhood Chain, World Chain and X Layer, the claim mint list of X Layer, and a dense receipt sample for Base and Robinhood Chain.
leads.why: These searches cover recent windows only, and the two networks with the most claim mints (29.7 million and 9.9 million) were sampled with a lighter rule because of endpoint limits.

leads.question: Part (c) of lead L-318: list native takes whose recipient is not the caller. This needs trace_filter or an explorer export of internal transactions of the PoolManager.
leads.why: Native takes leave no log outside Arc. This unit saw them only through wrapper Deposit logs, through traces of sampled claim mints and through Arc's native logs.

leads.question: Which factory or template produced the tokens that grant the helpers 0xd8e11826e82619bf49c58c05f26c8e00b0b64ea4 on Ethereum and 0xa25c886dced0e8fc0129082bf597381ea073c925 on BNB Smart Chain an allowance from the PoolManager, and how many pooled tokens of that template still hold a PoolManager balance?
leads.why: The same selector 0x73ed6b13 removed the PoolManager balance of 12 tokens on Ethereum and 18 on BNB Smart Chain. Live tokens of the template can be listed before they are used.

leads.question: Does the deployed PositionManager offer a way to remove liquidity when the PoolManager cannot pay one of the two tokens, for example by taking that side as an ERC-6909 claim or by clearing it?
leads.why: For the pools of MAGA, MEME, BITCOIN, ELX, SNI and DEAD the token side cannot be paid by take. Core allows mint and clear (src/PoolManager.sol:310-329), and whether ordinary liquidity providers can reach them decides if their other currency is frozen.

leadResults.answer: (a) Claim mints. I listed every ERC-6909 mint log on 20 networks over the whole history that the endpoints serve and on X Layer over 400,000 blocks: 53.3 million logs in total, of which 29.7 million on Base, 9.9 million on Robinhood Chain and 5.2 million on Unichain. Receipts of sample transactions for each caller and currency pair show unexplained mints on Polygon only, in the three known ids. New facts for F-066: sATH now has 151 mints, all sent by 0x34b6daa3c6b68c1a12b6e6f9e89ca6c0f7861d99 through two contracts, and the third contract called between sync and settle is the staking contract 0x98d21b8e6bf0c1d2dfb0e3fcb82035095dcdd7de with rebase() (trace of 0x5cc3e1803b3990c9a9d93749c855c91117a32c1ae3b26482ab341befa182c2cf); sLGNS stands at 661 mints to six recipients from 636 one use contracts and nine senders, 28 of them in the last seven days. No other network and no other token shows this trace, including sNVB and sSAC on BNB Smart Chain over the whole history and USDI and AMPL on Ethereum. Native claim mints without a pool event are paid by value in every checked case. (b) and (d) Round trips and unexplained outflows. A census of 0.5 to 30 days per network found flash use of take in ordinary tokens only, and no take that is followed by a larger credit. The flagged outflows are protocol fee collection, the Polygon claim mints, Arc's native log mirror, spoof tokens and one real case. (c) Native takes to third parties cannot be listed from logs. The cases seen are takes into the wrapper between sync and settle, which are zero sum, and Arc payouts that are matched by claim burns. What is new and lowers a recorded balance: on Base an ordinary account took the PoolManager's whole DEAD balance through the token's claimIdleTokens (third contract DeadToken 0xf0197f10ea542a67914ecc0ec5304dc9df1faf6f, no sync or settle involved); on Arbitrum One the owner of PUSD burned 41,000 PUSD of the PoolManager's balance; and on Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, Polygon, Unichain, Elysium and Arbitrum One token authors burned or moved the PoolManager's balance of about 150 tokens. In the sLGNS, sATH, sKLIMA, USDI and AMPL cases the amount was surplus that belonged to nobody. In the DEAD, PUSD and token author cases the amount was a balance that pools record, and the PoolManager's balance afterwards is lower than what pools record. Ranked by amount within what can be compared. Removed from a recorded balance by an unprivileged account: 14,899.78 DEAD on Base (unpriced). Destroyed by an issuer: 41,000 PUSD on Arbitrum One (41,000 USD if the token held its peg, which I did not check). Removed by token authors: 25,231,970 MAGA, 87,087,301 MEME and 806,756,916 BITCOIN on Ethereum, 601,450,442 CLU on Elysium, and smaller amounts for about 150 more tokens, all unpriced. Booked from unaccounted surplus as claims: 20,418.69 sLGNS (about 3,300 USD at the cycle 4 price), 329.79 sATH and 0.0102 sKLIMA on Polygon. The live PoolManagers are other bytecode than a build of this checkout, so these traces describe tokens and chains and say nothing about a defect in this build.
